beats.lead: A graphics card only has one job.
beats.text: It paints pixels onto a screen, over and over, very fast.
beats.note: In the early 2000s, researchers found a way to make it do something else entirely: ordinary arithmetic.

beats.lead: There was no button for that.
beats.text: So they disguised the maths as a picture.
beats.note: A grid of numbers became a texture. A calculation became a shader painting that texture onto a surface no one would ever actually look at.

beats.name: Two separate research teams
beats.role: Working independently and without knowing about each other, Krüger and Westermann, and separately Bolz, Farmer, Grinspun and Schröder, got graphics chips solving real linear algebra faster than a CPU could, using the same trick, at the same time.

beats.lead: For years, this stayed a workaround.
beats.text: Every calculation still had to be smuggled through a graphics language built for rendering, not maths.
beats.note: Programmers wrote in OpenGL or Direct3D and simply never drew anything with the result.

beats.name: CUDA
beats.role: NVIDIA's answer: a way to write directly for the graphics chip's raw parallel math, released in November, with no disguise required.

beats.text: Long before AI needed it, the graphics chip had already been tricked into doing sums.

beats.line: The pixel chip that became a math coprocessor.
